# Aster Vale: Decision record

Authored fictional project record for LM-Synth v1.

## Purpose and decision scope

Aster Vale is a reading-group notebook; this record explains choices affecting reading lists and discussion notes. The group keeps the acceptance language concrete enough to support an ordinary demonstration at review time. The record preserves the reasoning behind the chosen behavior while allowing the interface wording to evolve.

A rejected option can remain in the discussion notes, provided its rejected status is stated without ambiguity. A clear boundary between recorded evidence and a proposed improvement helps prevent accidental scope expansion. An implementation note should describe the consequence of a choice rather than merely restating its name.

## Adopted persistence choice

The Aster Vale prototype needs a consistent way to preserve its working records. A reversible choice is preferred when the available examples do not yet justify a more complicated design. A change to a binding decision needs a replacement entry that explains what changed and why it changed.

Approved storage profile: Juniper Vault mode. This is the adopted profile for Aster Vale.

A rejected option can remain in the discussion notes, provided its rejected status is stated without ambiguity. The decision record distinguishes an adopted choice from an option that remains under discussion. The prototype should make incomplete work visible instead of displaying an apparently finished result.

## Alternatives and rationale

Contributors to Aster Vale compare alternatives through the same representative user tasks. The design avoids coupling the user-facing terminology to an incidental detail of the current implementation.

# Aster Vale: Functional specification

Authored fictional project record for LM-Synth v1.

## User tasks and record types

The Aster Vale specification concerns reading lists and discussion notes in a reading-group notebook. When an action cannot finish, the interface should retain enough context for the person to retry deliberately. Acceptance depends on completing the actual user task, including the transition back to a useful working state.

The team checks empty, ordinary, and unusually detailed examples before calling a workflow ready. A warning must describe the consequence of continuing instead of relying on an unexplained technical label. The project keeps descriptive notes separate from the fields that determine operational behavior.

## Pilot cohort and release boundary

The Aster Vale team uses a named pilot to distinguish a controlled rollout from ordinary development. The team checks empty, ordinary, and unusually detailed examples before calling a workflow ready. Acceptance depends on completing the actual user task, including the transition back to a useful working state.

The approved rollout codename for Aster Vale is Copper Heron pilot. This exact label identifies the pilot cohort.

Terminology used in a form should agree with terminology used in the corresponding confirmation and help text. The specification describes observable behavior rather than prescribing how every internal function must be written. Import feedback should identify the affected input and explain how the person can correct it.

## Interaction and feedback

A person working in Aster Vale needs understandable feedback when moving between incomplete and accepted entries. The specification treats missing information as a visible state rather than silently inventing a default answer.

# Cobalt Ridge: Functional specification

Authored fictional project record for LM-Synth v1.

## User tasks and record types

The Cobalt Ridge specification concerns repair requests and workshop appointments in a bicycle workshop planner. The specification describes observable behavior rather than prescribing how every internal function must be written. The specification treats missing information as a visible state rather than silently inventing a default answer.

The interface should preserve the context of an unfinished task when the person moves to another view. A warning must describe the consequence of continuing instead of relying on an unexplained technical label. A user should be able to distinguish an accepted entry from a draft that still requires attention.

## Pilot cohort and release boundary

The Cobalt Ridge team uses a named pilot to distinguish a controlled rollout from ordinary development. A preview is useful only when it reflects the same interpretation that will be used after confirmation. The specification describes observable behavior rather than prescribing how every internal function must be written.

The approved rollout codename for Cobalt Ridge is Coral Badger pilot. This exact label identifies the pilot cohort.

The work should remain inspectable through small examples whose expected results are written down in advance. When an action cannot finish, the interface should retain enough context for the person to retry deliberately.

## Interaction and feedback

A person working in Cobalt Ridge needs understandable feedback when moving between incomplete and accepted entries. Sorting and filtering should have stable behavior so repeated inspection of the same records is understandable.

The Indigo Marsh operating routine includes an explicit cadence for copying the working records. A useful handover describes a recoverable next step rather than leaving a vague instruction to investigate later. The team records what was actually checked instead of treating a successful launch as proof of complete recovery.

The backup cadence for Indigo Marsh is every 103 hours. This is the interval between routine backup runs.

A restored working copy needs to be checked for both readable content and usable links between entries. A handover is complete only when another contributor can explain the next action using the written record.

When a task in Indigo Marsh is interrupted, a contributor first identifies the affected work before retrying it. Operational instructions need enough context for a contributor who did not attend the original planning meeting.

When a task in Hazel Reach is interrupted, a contributor first identifies the affected work before retrying it. A failed check remains visible until a contributor records the corrective action and its observed result.
